title: Parents warned of lifelong risks as students 'subcontracting learning' to AI
source_used: ABC News Australia (own reporting, full text read)
key_facts: The Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO), Australia's government-owned national education research body funded jointly by the Commonwealth and state governments, issued advice to teachers, school leaders and policymakers on 14 Oct 2026.
AERO reviewed studies from Australia and overseas on the risks and benefits of AI and warned schools to use AI 'sparingly' or risk students' lifelong learning outcomes.
CEO Dr Jenny Donovan described 'cognitive outsourcing': relying on the tool to do the thinking, a particular risk for novice learners.
She said studies overseas showed students who used AI could not replicate their results in an exam without it.
AERO says AI should be avoided completely in the first three years of primary school and only used carefully after that, together with established teaching practices such as explicit instruction.

Donovan said AI should be introduced in high school because it will matter in higher education, and praised tools such as NSW's own generative AI tool that guides students through reasoning instead of giving answers.
She asked parents to limit students' unfettered access to tools like ChatGPT at home.
Education Minister Jason Clare, citing weak Australian PISA results, said screen time in schools should be wound back, 'a bit of a digital detox'.
quote_evidence: Schools and teachers across Australia have been warned to use AI "sparingly" in the classroom or risk students' lifelong learning outcomes.

why_it_matters_hint: Australia's national education research body is telling schools and parents to limit AI because it may let students skip the thinking that builds knowledge.
notes: Single outlet (ABC); the AERO document itself and the studies it reviewed were not seen. Advice only, not a rule.
